summary: Place the behavior in one `assistant` capability. Share generation policy, provider failure classification, and safe error codes, but keep HTTP/SSE and job outcomes channel-native. A dedicated POST Route Handler is required because it owns Web Request/Response streaming, cancellation, header commitment, and SSE failures; a Server Action cannot preserve those lifecycle properties. Next.js explicitly supports streaming from Route Handlers using Web Streams ([Route Handler reference](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route)).

tree.purpose: Thin POST boundary: authenticate, validate prompt, create request context, invoke the stream surface, and return its Response.
Framework-neutral generation policy. Accepts typed input, identity, AbortSignal, and the model port; returns a typed asynchronous token sequence/final outcome.
Capability-shaped provider seam such as `startGeneration(...)`; exposes normalized tokens and failures, never provider SDK objects.
Closed failure taxonomy with safe public codes and job disposition metadata; distinguishes expected failures from unexpected exceptions.
Server-only SDK/HTTP adapter. Validates provider data, forwards AbortSignal, redacts details, and maps provider errors into capability failures.
SSE adapter owning first-event buffering, commit state, idle timer, cancellation composition, event serialization, and report-once handling.
Job adapter invoking the same generation operation and mapping normalized outcomes to acknowledge, retry, or dead-letter.
Narrow server-only public surface consumed by the Route Handler; wires generation, provider, clock, and reporter.
Narrow worker-facing public surface; exposes the job invocation contract without exposing internals.
Browser-safe POST/fetch client that parses `token`, `done`, and `failure` SSE events and aborts fetch when the UI cancels.
Browser public surface exporting the stream consumer and public event types.

flows: Browser: UI calls `client.consumeStream(prompt, signal)` → POST `/api/assistant/stream` → Route Handler authenticates and validates → `assistant/stream.ts` → `application/generate.ts` → `model-port.ts` → `remote-model-provider.ts`. The POST Route Handler is appropriate because Route Handlers use standard Web Request/Response APIs and support streaming responses.

Pre-commit: the stream adapter starts generation and awaits/buffers the first token or terminal outcome before returning `Response`. Validation/auth failures and expected provider startup failures can therefore become safe non-2xx JSON responses. An unexpected exception is reported once by this outer boundary and becomes a generic 500 response.

Committed stream: return `Response(ReadableStream)` with `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, `Cache-Control: no-cache`, and anti-buffering configuration appropriate to deployment. Emit `event: token` frames, then one `event: done`. After commitment, an expected or unexpected failure cannot change HTTP status: emit exactly one sanitized `event: failure` frame and close. Unexpected failures are reported once here; application and provider layers never report.

Cancellation: compose the incoming `request.signal`, the stream consumer's `cancel()` signal, and an idle-timeout AbortController into the signal passed through the application port to the provider request. Any source aborts provider work and closes the stream; client cancellation is not reported as an outage.

Idle timeout: arm while waiting for provider activity, reset after every accepted provider token/activity, and clear on completion, failure, or cancellation. It aborts only a silent interval; it is not an absolute duration cap, so a healthy long stream continues indefinitely.

Background job: worker imports `assistant/job.ts` → job boundary validates payload and establishes service identity/job context → `job-runner.ts` invokes the same `generate.ts` policy and provider seam, consuming tokens into the job's required sink/result. Success acknowledges. Normalized transient/rate-limit failures request retry with bounded attempt/backoff policy; permanent input/auth/policy failures dead-letter immediately; exhausted transient failures dead-letter. Unexpected exceptions are reported once by the job boundary and follow the job's retry/exhaustion policy.

decisions.choice: Do not use one wrapper across HTTP, SSE, and jobs.
decisions.rationale: The shared pieces are failure codes, redaction, provider mapping, and generation policy. HTTP needs status/body, an already-committed stream needs in-band events, and a job needs retry/dead-letter disposition. Wrapping all three would erase required lifecycle state.

decisions.choice: Use a dedicated POST Route Handler; do not route streaming through a Server Action.
decisions.rationale: This is a browser-owned streaming read with explicit Response headers, Web Stream cancellation, and commit-aware failure behavior. Those are Route Handler responsibilities, whereas Server Actions are mutation/RPC boundaries.

decisions.choice: Never automatically retry an ordinary browser stream request after emission begins.
decisions.rationale: Retry could duplicate tokens or repeat provider effects. Only a failure before commitment may be safely retried under an explicit idempotency policy; jobs apply their own attempt policy.

decisions.choice: Make `generate.ts` the reusable policy boundary and keep lifecycle mechanics outside it.
decisions.rationale: Deleting it would move generation policy and failure branching into both HTTP and job callers, while cancellation, idle timing, reporting, and delivery outcomes remain channel-specific.

decisions.choice: Only the outer active channel reports unexpected failures.
decisions.rationale: The Route Handler/stream adapter or job boundary has the complete request/job context and can guarantee one report; inner policy and provider adapters only throw or return classified failures.

risks: Some proxies and hosting platforms buffer streaming responses; verify end-to-end streaming and disable proxy buffering where applicable ([Next.js self-hosting guidance](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/self-hosting)).
First-event buffering delays header commitment until provider startup is known; bound that wait with the same idle mechanism.
SSE framing must escape/serialize payloads defensively and expose only stable safe codes—never raw provider messages, credentials, or stack traces.
If provider cancellation is not honored promptly, aborted browser requests can continue consuming provider resources; test the adapter with real disconnects.
Retry classification must be explicit and bounded so permanent failures do not loop and transient failures eventually dead-letter.
